title: Short Stuff: Figs & Wasps
summary: Short Stuff episode on fig wasps and the edible fig. Chuck and Josh explain the mutualistic relationship between fig wasps and figs (co-evolved over about sixty million years). Edible figs (Calimyrna, grown commercially in California, with the wasp imported from Turkey) produce a syconium; male trees produce an inedible caprifig. A female wasp exits a male fig, picks up pollen, and enters a female fig, where she loses her wings, dies, and is broken down by the enzyme ficin inside the fig. Her ovipositor is too short to lay eggs in female figs, so she pollinates them and dies in the process. Farmers separate male and female trees to prevent seed-driven bursting and control wasp populations. The hosts debate whether figs are self-pollinating (Josh) and discuss that eating figs means eating a bit of wasp, USDA ketchup fruit fly egg standards, and a "wasp becomes fig" t-shirt joke.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to fig wasps
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short episode, sitting in for Dave. Chuck says the hosts did not cover fig wasps in the earlier wasp episode, and notes that edible figs are grown commercially in California and imported from Turkey along with their wasp.

segments.title: Mutualism between figs and fig wasps
segments.summary: The hosts describe the co-evolved mutualistic relationship over about sixty million years: the fig depends on the wasp and the wasp on the fig. Edible figs are a syconium, not a true fruit. Female trees bear edible figs, male trees bear inedible caprifigs, and a female wasp must enter the syconium to pollinate them.

segments.title: Wasp life cycle and eating figs
segments.summary: A female wasp loses her wings entering the syconium and dies there; enzyme ficin breaks her down, so eating a fig means eating a little broken-down wasp. Her life cycle starts in a male fig, where she mates with a wingless male, picks up pollen, and then enters either a male or female fig. In a female fig her ovipositor is too short to lay eggs, so she pollinates it and dies.

segments.title: Debate over fig self-pollination and farmers separating trees
segments.summary: Chuck explains farmers separate male and female trees to control wasp reproduction. Josh disputes this, saying some figs are self-pollinating and hermaphroditic. Chuck cites an interviewed farmer. They agree to disagree.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before returning to content.

segments.title: Insects in food and USDA ketchup standards
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that bugs are present in many fruits and that the USDA allows some insect activity. They cite a USDA grade for tomato ketchup allowing up to thirty fruit fly eggs per one hundred grams, and question how the count is enforced.

segments.title: Farm control of wasps and seed bursting
segments.summary: Chuck explains farmers separate trees over distances to keep seeds from bursting the fruit and to control how many female wasps reach the correct plant; wasps are delivered by mail in paper sacks. Josh jokes about vegans and tells listeners that eating figs means eating some insects.

segments.title: Wasp becomes fig sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts joke about a wasp becomes fig t-shirt and close the episode with the iHeartRadio production credit.
